To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Feeding initiates mitosis of the epithelial cells of the duodenum and esophagus in newly hatched chickens.
feeding initiates cellular proliferation in the duodena and the esophaga of starved chickens by stimulating cells from G1 to enter the S phase of the mitotic cell cycle.
the cell cycle of the esophageal epithelium in the chicken is divided in two parts, G1 and G2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the cell cycle in the epithelial tissues of the gastrointestinal tract.
the initiation of cell division in the esophagus and duodenum.
the regulation of cell proliferation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the initiation of the cell division process is a result of the stimulation of the G1 cells by feeding.
the initiation of mitosis following starvation is a function of the cell cycle in which the cells are held.
starvation does not affect the duration of the cell cycle but it does affect its distribution among the different cell cycle phases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
feeding stimulates cell division in the duodena and esophagi of starved animals, and that this stimulation is initiated in the G1 part and the G2 part of the cell cycle, respectively.
feeding of starved animals initiates mitosis by a direct stimulation of cells in G1 and a simultaneous stimulation of cells in both G1 and G2.
starvation causes a depression of cellular proliferation, but the mechanism of this effect is complex and may vary from organ to organ.
The main takeaway from our work is that
feeding stimulates cell division in the duodena and the esophagus, but in the latter tissue, some of the cells are held back in G1 or G2.
the cell cycle is a very sensitive indicator of the metabolic state of the animal.
feeding initiates the cell cycle in the duodenal epithelium by a G1 stimulus and in the esophageal epithelium in two ways: by a G1 or G2 stimulus.
